analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.65 an hour over two years.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.65 an hour, with 49 cosponsors, died in a House subcommittee and never got a vote before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in three steps: to $5.75 shortly after passage, to $6.25 on January 1, 2003, and to $6.65 on January 1, 2004 [S2][S3]. It also would have applied the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, phasing the wage there up from $3.55 an hour [S2][S3]. The House never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the minimum wage would get a raise in three steps, reaching $6.65 an hour by 2004 — about a 29% increase over the $5.15 rate then in effect. Workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, whose minimum wage was lower and whose islands had been exempt from the federal wage floor, would see their wage phased up to the federal level [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage workers, including in the Marianas

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps — $5.75 within about two months of enactment, $6.25 beginning January 1, 2003, and $6.65 beginning January 1, 2004 — up from the $5.15 rate then in law [S2][S3].

Makes the federal minimum wage apply to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, with a transition starting at $3.55 an hour and rising 50 cents every six months until it matches the federal wage [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ minimum-wage workers — especially restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service employers — would bear higher payroll costs, some of which could be passed to customers through prices. Employers in the Northern Mariana Islands, including its garment and hotel industries, would face the largest increase as the wage floor rose from $3.55 to the federal level [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers, especially restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: Higher mandated wages raise costs for small businesses and low-margin employers, and some economists argue they can reduce hours or entry-level jobs; in the Northern Mariana Islands, the transition from $3.55 to the full federal wage posed a sharp cost shock for local garment and hotel employers [S2][S3].
The bill set a single national wage floor with no regional cost-of-living adjustment, so the same rate applied to high-cost cities and low-cost rural areas alike [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and large for the workers affected: a roughly 29% wage increase phased over two years, plus the first federal wage floor ever applied to the Northern Mariana Islands. The main cost falls on employers of low-wage labor and, indirectly, on consumers through prices; the strongest honest objection is the risk of reduced hours or entry-level hiring for some workers, though the phased schedule softened that. On balance the gains to low-wage workers clearly outweigh the diffuse, modest costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, where it sat until Congress ended in January 2003 — no markup, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. David Bonior (D-MI) introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2002 on May 22, 2002, joined by Democratic leaders including Reps. Gephardt, Pelosi, and George Miller [S1][S3].
The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.65 an hour by 2004 and applied the federal wage floor to the Northern Mariana Islands [S2][S3].
It attracted 49 cosponsors — 48 of 208 House Democrats and the chamber's sole Independent; no House Republican cosponsored it [S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced, and on October 3, 2002, referred it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last recorded action before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum wage — restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses, plus the garment and hotel industries of the Northern Mariana Islands — kept the existing $5.15 federal floor (and $3.05 in the Marianas) rather than facing the phased increase. The roughly 5-7 million workers who would have gotten raises did not.

for.name: Rep. David Bonior
for.role: U.S. Representative, D-MI; House Minority Whip
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push to raise the minimum wage to $6.65 an hour

for.name: House Democratic leadership (Gephardt, Pelosi, Miller and others)
for.role: Original cosponsors, including the Minority Leader and Minority Whip
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral, sending it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and never scheduled a markup or vote before Congress ended

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never acted on the bill; the minimum wage increase never received a committee vote or floor consideration

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the 107th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent — 48 of 208 House Democrats plus 1 of 1 Independents — and no House Republican signed on; the Republican majority never scheduled action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have raised their payroll costs roughly 29% per minimum-wage hour by 2004. Their interest in holding the wage at $5.15 ran directly against the raise workers would have received [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and hotel industries
industries.note: The bill would have ended the islands' decades-long exemption from the federal wage floor, phasing their minimum wage from $3.55 up to the federal level. The Marianas' garment factories had long relied on wage rates far below the U.S. mainland floor [S2][S3].
